albert-johnson-evergreen-1910-08-06.A2:
Negro Murderer Captured
Bay Minette, August 4.—(Special.)—Word has been received here that a negro answering the description of the one who murdered Jesse Baldwin of Conecuh county, near Wilcox, about a month ago, was captured this morning by Riley Hubbard, section foreman, between Bay Minette and Almore, on the Louisville and Nashville railroad, at about 8:30 o'clock. After the capture the negro confessed the crime and named three others who were implicated in the affair. Sheriff Irwin of Evergreen was notified at once and met Deputy Sheriff McGill, into whose hands the negro was placed, at Pollard.
albert-johnson-evergreen-1910-08-06.A3:
SOLDIERS OF CONECUH GUARD BLACK QUINTET Mob Surrounds Jail at Evergreen. THREATEN VIOLENCE FOR DEATH OF JESSE BALDWIN When Troops Appear, Angered Citizens Disperse. SHERIFF IRWIN COMES TO MONTGOMERY SATURDAY MORNING, THINKING DANGER OF LYNCHING OVER AFTER FIRST ARREST.
Evergreen, Aug. 7.—(Special.)—At 3 o'clock this morning the streets of Evergreen in the vicinity of the Conecuh County jail are being patrolled by members of Company "K," 1st regiment, Alabama National Guard, of Evergreen, under command of Capt. T. M. Bruner.

Leaving the city in a northerly direction is a body of 100 or 125 men, who, during the early hours of the night, surrounded the Conecuh County jail, fired occasional shots, and hinted at violence against five negroes held in connection with the death of Jesse Baldwin, an aged farmer, who was murdered at Wilcox Station, July 7.

The mob formed at 12:30 o'clock, and did not disperse until after 3 o'clock, when the military assumed charge of the situation. It is believed that the members of the mob are from the country sections, and not from Evergreen.

When it was found that a mob was forming, the Evergreen troops were ordered into their armory. With them were Deputy Sheriffs E. C. Hinds and H. F. Nalls. These had the keys to the jail.

Jesse Baldwin's body was found near the back door of his home one month ago, his skull crushed by a blow from a hoe. He was known to have kept large sums of money about his home, and this money was missing. Conecuh County officers have been working on the case, and have captured five suspects. Albert Johnson was taken Wednesday in the lower part of Escambia County, and returned to Evergreen by Sheriff Irwin. Charley Henderson, another negro, was captured Friday. John Manuel, Charley Manuel and Jerry Mims, three other negroes, were taken and placed in jail Saturday morning.

The jail about which the mob assembled is considered almost mob proof. It is a two-story structure, about 40 by 60 feet in dimension. The outer door is of steel and opens outward. Behind that is another steel door which opens inward. To reach the cells, it is necessary to climb a winding stairway and open another steel door against which it is impossible to direct any kind of a battering ram.

Sheriff Irwin came to Montgomery Saturday night, and was at a local hotel when news of the mob was conveyed to him. He declared that he had expected trouble several nights during the last week, but believed that the excitement had subsided when he left Evergreen Saturday. He declared that there was no evidence of feeling when he left the town Saturday afternoon.

The Conecuh Sheriff expressed confidence in the two officers in charge, and also in the military force. He believed that the officials would be able to cope with the situation. He made preparations to leave Montgomery for Evergreen on the early morning train Sunday.
albert-johnson-evergreen-1910-08-06.A5:
THE WEATHER. Washington, Aug. 7--Forecast for Alabama: Local showers Monday and Tuesday; light to moderate variable winds. RUSH NEGROES FROM CONECUH Prisoners Taken to Mobile Jail. TROOPS RELIEVED FROM DUTY Another Suspect Arrested by Members of Company. AUTHORITIES IN CONTROL OF SIT-UATION, AND BELIEVE DANGER OF LYNCHING DISAPPEARED WITH NEGROES' RE- MOVAL.
ing that another attempt would be made by a mob to storm the Conecuh county jail and lynch two negro men who were held there on a charge of having murdered Jesse Baldwin, an aged man on his farm near Wilcox about a month ago, Sheriff H. F. Irwin Sunday secured permission from Circuit Judge J. C. Richardson at Greenville, to remove Albert Johnson and John Manuel, the two negroes, to the Mobile county jail for safekeeping. The negroes were taken to Mobile Sunday afternoon by Sheriff Irwin and Deputy Sheriff Hinds.

When the 9:40 train from Montgomery arrived in Evergreen Sunday morning, Lieutenant J. C. Cheney, Jr., and Private G. R. Farnham, Jr., members of Company "K," went into a coach in which several negroes were riding and arrested Frank Mitchell, who is charged with having alced and abetted Albert Johnson and John Mitchell and John Manuel in evading arrest by the sheriff of Conecuh county. Mitchell was taken immediately to the Conecuh county jail, and there locked up with Charley Manuel, Jerry Mims and Charley Henderson, all negroes, who also are charged with having alded the two alleged murderers in evading arrest for several days.

Remus White, the third negro who was accused of taking part in the murder of Jesse Baldwin, was shot and killed several days ago by a deputy sheriff, who was in the act of arresting him.

Mob Came From North.

It was stated in Evergreen today that the mob of Saturday night came from the vicinity of Owassa and from the neighborhood in which Baldwin had lived prior to his murder. There, feeling is said to be bitter against the negroes. There were about 100 members in the mob, each one armed either with a shotgun or a Winchester rifle. Had not the local company of militia formed a protecting line about the jail before the arrival of the mob, serious consequence might have resulted.

Train No. 3 which arrived in Evergreen 10:45 o'clock Saturday night brought the information from Owassa that a large crowd of men, armed and on foot, would soon attack the county jail with a view to lynching all the negroes concerned in the murder of Jesse Baldwin.

This report reached Captain T. M. Bruner of Company "K," A. N. G., and he immediately called together all the available members of his company to arm themselves and report for duty at the jail.

While the members of the militia company, along with deputy sheriff were in the company armory, several members of the mob came into the room, and demanded that the deputy sheriff turn over to them the keys to the jail, according to Lieutenant Cheney and other members of the company. This was refused, and the members of the mob were ordered to get out of the building. No member of the militia recognized the men, although they were not masked.

The militia men then hurried to the jail, and had hardly formed a protecting line about the prison when the mob appeared. When the mob come within forty feet of the line of soldiers they were ordered to halt, and send one man forward to arbitrate with Captain Bruner. This was done. the mob leader whose name would not be divulged, asking that the keys to the jail be turned over to him. Again this demand was refused, and the refusal was accompanied by an order to the mob to disperse.

Trouble is Threatened.

At this juncture it seemed that trouble of a serious nature would occur, as the members of the mob began cocking their guns and mumbling in dissatisfied tones, according to statements of the militia men. After about half an hour, however, the mob quietly dispersed and disappeared in a northerly direction.

The militia was then disbanded, Lieutenant Cheney and Private Farnham being left on duty to guard the jail in case any members of the mob should return.

No further trouble was experienced however, and at 2:20 o'clock Sunday afternoon Lieutenant Cheney and Private Farnham formed a military escort and accompanied Deputy Sheriff Hinds with Albert Johnson and John Manuel as his prisoners to the railroad station. Sheriff Irwin coming from Montgomery, remained on the train and accompanied Deputy Hinds and the negroes to the Mobile county jail at Mobile.

Although some rumors were abroad in Evergreen during the early afternoon Sunday that a mob much larger than that of Saturday night, would storm the jail Sunday night, county officials were of the opinion that the removal of Johnson and Manuel against whom feeling was bitterest, to Mobile, would serve to deter such action.

Confesses Presence at Crime.

Mobile, Aug. 7.—Albert Johnson, the negro who, with John Manuel, is charged with the murder of Jesse Baldwin three weeks ago near Evergreen, and who was brought, with Manuel, to this city today by Sheriff Irvin of Conecuh County, after having escaped the wrath of a mob which ineffectually stormed the jail at Evergreen, confessed today that he was at the scene of the murder when Jesse Baldwin was done to death. He accused Manuel of having struck some of the blows which ended fatally for the aged farmer, and also stated that Remus White used a hoe on the old man, thus equally aiding in causing his death.

Shortly after the arrival here of Sheriff Irvin with his prisoners, a local reporter, in the presence of several deputy sheriffs, asked Johnson and Manuel whether or not they had had any hand in the killing of Jesse Bald-

accused of being one of the murderers, admitted that he was at the house of Baldwin when the old farmer was killed, and that he saw the murder committed, but he said he did not strike a blow, but merely looked on while the others did the killing. When he was asked who did strike the blow that killed the old man, he pointed at John Manuel and said that he was the one who had the club with which part of the killing was done; and that Remus White, the negro who was killed by Deputy Sheriff Noel three weeks ago, was the man who had the hoe, one of the weapons with which the crime was committed. As soon as Johnson finished telling this part of the story, Manuel called him a liar, and said that he (Manuel) had not been present at the killing at all. Sheriff Irvin stated that he would not be surprised if Johnson told the truth, as he believed that the killing had been done by more than one man.
albert-johnson-evergreen-1910-08-06.A7:
MILITIA CALLED OUT
TO PREVENT LYNCHINGS
Mob Surrounds Alabama Jail, Making Threats Against Two Negroads Alabama Jail, Making Threats Against Two Negroes.
EVERGREEN, Ala., August 8.—Threatening to lynch Albert Johnson and John Manuel, negroes, who were in jail here on the charge of being implicated in the killing of Jesse Baldwin, an aged farmer, at Wilcox station July 7, a mob gathered at 2:30 o'clock yesterday morning and surrounded the jail, with the evident object of carrying their threats into execution.

Sheriff J. F. Irwin, however, forestalled any attempt at violence by calling on the officers of the local military company, Company K, 1st Infantry, Alabama National Guard, for assistance, and the appearance of the troops served soon afterward to quell the mob spirit, the men returning to their homes.

Fearing a further outbreak last night Sheriff Irwin and a deputy took the two negroes to Mobile for safekeeping.

Charley Henderson, Charley and Jerry Mims, three other negroes, remain in jail in connection with the same case, but it is believed that danger of violence has passed.

Hold Pursuing Crowd at Bay.

DRESDEN, Tenn., August 8.—Three young brothers, named Alexander, after having slain the son of a neighbor in the course of a picnic near Kenton, Tenn., held the pursuing crowd at bay until they made their escape, but were afterward captured by deputy sheriffs and put in jail at Kenton, where they were threatened with lynching by infuriated neighbors Saturday night.

The affair grew out of a crap game. Robert Simmons, jr., having won all the money, mounted his horse to ride away, when one of the Alexanders, it is said, seized the bridle rein, another stabbed Simmons, and when he fell to earth the third Alexander rushed up and beat him with a club. The picnickers rushed to the rescue, but the three Alexanders drew revolvers and got away for the time. Fear. Fear of lynching has abated.
albert-johnson-evergreen-1910-08-06.A15:
ARRIVAL OF TROOPS
SAVES NEGROES FOM MOB
EVERGREEN, Ala., Aug. 8. — Order was restored Sunday morning here, and company K. First infantry, of this place, has been removed from duty.

Fearing a further outbreak last night, Sheriff J. F. Irwin and Deputy Sheriff E. C. Hinds this afternoon took Albert Johnson and John Manuel to Mobile for safe keeping. These two nogroes are held in connection with the murder of Jesse Baldwin, an aged farmer at Wilcox station, July 7.

Charley Henderson, Charley Manuel and Jerry Mims, three other negroes, remain in the jail in connection with the same case, but it is believed that the authorities are in full control of the situation, and that friends of the dead man will allow the law to take its course.
albert-johnson-evergreen-1910-08-06.A23:
BY THE SOLDIERS
Attack on Jail Checked in Alabama.

Evergreen, Ala., August 7. —Order was restored this morning here and Company K. First Infantry, of this place has been removed from duty. Fearing a further outbreak tonight, Sheriff J. F. Irwin and Deputy Sheriff E. C. Hinds this afternoon took Albert Johnson and John Manuel to Mobile for safe-keeping. These two negroes are held in connection with the murder of Jesse Baldwin, an aged farmer at Wilcox station July 7th.
Charley Henderson, Charley Manuel and Jerry Mims, three other negroes, remain in the jail in connection with the same case, but it is believed that the authorities are in full control of the situation, and that friends of the dead men will allow the law to take its course. The mob formed Sunday morning at 12:30 o'clock. Surrounding the jail the members fired shots and made threats against the black prisoners. The Evergreen company of infantry immediately was called to the armory. At 3 o'clock the mob was dispersed when the troops appeared and surrounded the jail, where they were on guard until the danger of the attack was passed.

NEGRO MURDERER
AGAIN CAPTURED
Florence, August 27.—(Special.)—Bob Hibble, the negro who jumped from a train moving 50 miles an hour between Barton and Cherokee and escaped Thursday from two Mississippi officers, with guns leveled on him, was captured this morning near Cherokee, and escaped Thursda
bob-hibble-cherokee-1910-08-07.A3:
Strong Inducements. Indianapolis News. Almost any lawyer would have taken an interest in the Indians at Mr. McMurray's regular interest rates. LEAPS FROM CAR WINDOW NEGRO WANTED FOR MURDER MAKES DARING ESCAPE. Jumps From Speeding Train. As Officers Enter Coach to Arrest Him, But is Not Injured.
Tuscumbia, Aug. 27.—(Special)—Bob Hibble, a negro, said to be a fugitive from Mississippi, and supposed to be the man wanted for the murder of Dewitt White, a white man of Attalla county, Mississippi, on August 19, made a daring and desperate dash for liberty yesterday on a passenger train running at least sixty miles an hour when confronted by officers who boarded the train at Cherokee, eighteen miles west of Tuscumbia, after having been wired by the train conductor that he had on his train a negro answering the description of the man wanted and for whom there is a $200 reward.

With drawn revolvers the officers entered the coach between Cehorkee and Barton, and demanded the negro to throw up his hands. Quick as a flash the negro threw himself out of an open window where he was sitting, while the train was making from fifty to sixty miles an hour, and so suddenly that the officers had no time to use their guns. The train was immediately stopped and backed to the point where the negro jumped, the officers believing that the man was either killed or badly injured by his desperate act, but instead there were no signs of the negro, and it is supposed he made his flying leap without injury. Nothing has been heard of him since.
bob-hibble-cherokee-1910-08-07.A4:
Wrong Negro Captured
Tuscumbia, August 30.—(Special.)—After risking his life by jumping from a fast moving train and being filled with buckshot as the supposed Bob Hibble, wanted in Attalla county, Mississippi, for the murder of Dewitt White, a deputy sheriff, officers who arrived from Attalla yesterday declared the negro prisoner at Cherokee to be the wrong man.
bob-hibble-cherokee-1910-08-07.A5:
Railway Sued For Damages
Tuscumbia, September 7.—(Special.)—The Southern railway is defendant in a unique suit for $3000 brought by Lassie Hamilton, a negress, in the Colbert county circuit court. The bill alleges that the plaintiff was a passenger on the defendant's train one night last month when officers boarded the train in search of Bob Hibble, wanted in Mississippi for murder. Guns were drawn on the negro and in her effort to get out of range of them the woman fell, hurting herself considerably. She further alleges that she was badly frightened and for the further injury done to her feeling by the profanity of an officer asks $3000 damages.

dick-lee-moreland-1910-08-26.A1:
Mob Talk
HEARD WHEN NEGRO STABBED WHITE MEN AT MORELAND
Dick Lee, a bad colored man, stabbee two white men, Emmett Netkirk and Huston Acre at Moreland last Friday, and for a while there was talk among the friends of the two men of making an effort to storm the jail here that night and lynch the negro. Cooler heads prevailed, however, and nothing was done.

The two white men are from the Green river section in Casey. It is said that they came to Moreland and sought work loading lumber, much of which had been done by the negroes. Lee became angry, it is said, and "went after" the white men with a large knife when they resented his remarks to them.

Sheriff W. L. McCarty arrested Lee who was brought to jail here. He is said to have a bad reputation and to have wielded his ready knife on previous occasions.
dick-lee-moreland-1910-08-26.A2:
Stays In Jail
DICK LEE UNABLE TO FURNISH
$500 BOND
Dick Lee, the negro who severely cut the white men, Akers and Neikirk, at Moreland, last week, was tried before County Judge Bailey here and held to await the action of the grand jury on his case His bond was fixed at $500, which he was unable to give, so he is the guest of Col. Dink Farmer, until the high tribunal assembles. The men he cut have sufficiently recovered from their injuries to be able to appear against him. Attorney T. J. Hill has been retained to defend Lee.
dick-lee-moreland-1910-08-26.A6: The Wayne County Outlook asks, who is "Dick Lee," the negro boy who was recently arrested at Stanford, upon the charge of stabbing two white men The boy's name is Dick Lee Hardin. He was born and reared near Columbia. He got into trouble here and left six or eight years ago. His mother lives near this place, and we understand has been to Stanford to see ner son since he got into trouble at that place.

event.A1:
NIGHT RIDER CASRS ARE CONTINUED Is Alleged They Took Oaths to Drive Negroes From Community.
Lonoke.—The night rider cases, which were set for trial in the Lonoke circuit court, which is now in session, have been continued for six months. The parties indicted are George Granberry, Vernon Leggett and Frank Reeder, on the charge of taking binding oaths for the purpose of intimidating negroes and riotous conspiracy. They are charged with having taken a negro out under the pretense of arrest and escorting him to the woods for a whipping. In going, the negro was made to say his prayers and the leader, stumbling over a leg, as the defendants state allower the negro a chance to escape, which he did, amidst a volley of shots, and has never been heard of since.

john-wayne-huntington-1910-08-29.A4:
NEGRO KILLS HIS BOSS WITH PICK
Harry Withrow, 33, section foreman on the Chesapeake & Ohio Railroad, was killed at Huntington at noon Saturday by Charles Clyburn, negro section hand, who had just been discharged.

Clyburn drove a pick into Withrow's back, killing him instantly. The negro is lodged in gail there but is being closely guarded to prevent lynching.

Thomas Wayne, the negro charged with murdering Mrs. John Aillis near Hinton, is in the same jail, and it is feared a mob may attempt to lynch both negroes.
john-wayne-huntington-1910-08-29.A5:
MOB CHEATED OF PREY.
Prisoners Spirited Away While Sheriff Argues.
HUNTINGTON, W. Va., August 29.—A mob of about 500, including 200 from Hinton, W. Va., gathered around the county jail here shortly after dark last night clamoring for the lives of Thomas Wayne, the negro charged with murdering Mrs. John Ailiff, at Quinnemont, and Charles Clyburn, another negro, who killed Harry Withrow, a railroad foreman, here Saturday.

Both men were placed in jail here for safe keeping. For half an hour Sheriff Harry Berger pleaded and threatened the mob, but apparently without effect.

Finally, realizing that the situation was serious, he took up a place on the steps of the jail. While he was arguing with the mob leaders his deputies spirited the prisoners away.

Their destination or whereabouts is unknown.
john-wayne-huntington-1910-08-29.A7:
ATTEMPT MADE TO LYNCH TWO MEN
HUNTINGTON, W. Va., Aug. 30. ~ Militiamen and sheriff's deputies today are guarding the county jail, following an attempt last night to lynch John Wayne and Charles Claybourne. The blacks are alleged to have committed a brutal murder.

Feeling against the prisoners and the negro population generally is so bitter that a race war is feared. It is probable that martial law will be declared. Several men involved in the attack on the jail are under arrest.

A special grand jury has been called and is investigating the outbreak.
john-wayne-huntington-1910-08-29.A9:
Huntington, W. Va., Rioters Use Clubs and Missiles. Martial Law Declared.
SHERIFF HELPLESS
CALLS IN MILITIA
Crowd Becomes More Threatening,
and Further Trouble Today
Is Feared.
The negroes are accused of murdering a white woman and fatally injuring her husband.

Wayne is charged with the murder of Mrs. John Alliff, near Quinnimont, and Clayburn is alleged to have murdered her husband near here last Saturday.

Mrs. Alliff was killed while she and her husband, who had been married but a few hours, were going to their home. The bridegroom was beaten unconscious and the bride's body was recovered from a brook by the road where the attack occurred, near Quinnimont.

Wayne confessed to having murdered Mrs. Alliff almost immediately after his capture and troops had to be called out then to save him from a mob. Wayne also confessed that before he killed Mrs. Alliff he seriously wounded her husband, who was a section foreman of the Chesapeake and Ohio railroad. Clayburn is charged with the murder of Charles Withrow, who also was a Chesapeake and Ohio foreman.

The mob in Huntington had been swollen to more than five thousand before noon today, and the authorities made frenzied appeals by wire for the immediate dispatch of more troops.

Mob Attacks Sheriff.

In a clash between the troops and the mob of 4,000 a score of persons were injured, some seriously, and fifty persons were arrested. The militiamen charged into the heart of the crowd, which fought back with clubs and missiles before being cowed for the time being.

The calling out of the troops followed a desperate attempt on the part of the local authorities to restore order.

Sheriff Harshmarger, surrounded by a force of regulars and special deputies, mounted the steps of the jail in an attempt to reason with the mob.
Sorties Against Jail.

Occasionally parties led sorties against the jail, but for the most part it was a waiting game till the sky began to lighten.

The arrival of the troops, brought here on special trains, brought matters to a climax. With bayonets fixed the soldiers tramped through the town to the jail, while jeering crowds lined the streets, at times showering them with missiles.

The main force was concentrated about the prison, but a strong police force was detailed to cover the rest of the town. All loiterers in the outlying districts were arrested.

This morning, after the clash in which the troops charged the mob, an appeal for re-enforcements was taken under consideration.

A mob gathered before the door of the jail in which Wayne and Clayburn were confined and battered down the doors last night. A force of police and deputy sheriffs who had been on guard charged the crowd and finally drove it back from the immediate vicinity of the jail.

Sheriff Harshbarger tried to calm the mob, urging it to let justice take its course and pledging his word that the negroes would meet with the extreme penalty for their crimes.

For a while it seemed as if the sheriff's efforts would be successful, but fresh recruits kept joining the ranks of the mob until shortly before daylight its frenzy broke bounds and another charge was made on the jail, driving the guard of police and deputies back into it.

Cut By Bayonets.
The sheriff then made an appeal for troops and two companies of State militia were hurried to the scene. They charged the mob and drove it from the jail after wounding several men with their bayonets and arresting fifty-seven.
Men from the outlying sections kept pouring into the town throughout the forenoon and the spirit of the mob grew more desperate as the day advanced.
Shortly before noon word was passed to the troops to be ready to repulse an attack on the jail and fears grew that there would be more bloodshed before night.
john-wayne-huntington-1910-08-29.A18:
A., WEDNESDAY. AUGUST 31, 1910
Harry Withrow Murdered.
C. & O. Section Foreman Harry Withrow met with an untimely death at Huntington about the noon hour last Saturday. He was foully murdered by a negro named Charley Clayburn. The crime stands without a particle of excuse whatever.

Clayburn, who is only 19 years old, came to this section from North Carolina, and had been working as a section hand on the hang in charge of Withrow, since the second of August. His work Saturday morning caused him to be reprimanded by Withrow. The reprimand angered the negro and he asked for his time. Withrow told his brother to make out Clayburn's time and pay him off at noon. When the time arrived to quit work for noon, the men picked up their tools and started toward the tool house near the passenger depot and a wrangle ensued between Clayburn and his foreman. Withrow told Clayburn to shut up and carry his tools on to the tool house, stooping as he made the remark to pick up a crow bar that lay on the ground nearby. As he stooped over the negro swung the heavy pick driving it through Withrow's spinal column and upward into the base of the brain. With a pitiful moan the victim of the enraged negro's wrath fell forward on his face. The pick stuck fast in his back.

Russell and George Withrow, brothers of the stricken man, quickly drew the awful weapon from his body and then leaving him in charge of others who gathered there, ran after the murderous negro. They soon caught the assassin and turned him over to the police who locked him in a cell in the county jail.

Withrow was taken to the hospital but lived only twelve hours after the assault.

The deceased was 33 years of age and is survived by a wife and one child. His wife was formerly Miss Myrtle Smith, the daughter of M. J. Smith, who was a citizen of Ceredo for many years and for a long time identified with the track work of the C. & O. but who now resides in Oklahoma. They had been married but four years.

The parents of the dead man reside at Coalton, Ky., where the body was taken for burial.

Clayburn has no parents, brothers, sisters or relatives of any character.

MOB ATTEMPTS TO LYNCH NEGROES.

A small mob formed Sunday night for the purpose of lynching the negroes—John Wayne and Charley Clayburn—but were thwarted, and on Monday night a mob of probably 2,500 people formed near the jail with the express purpose of putting to death the murderers. This mob was formed about 10:30 and for a couple of hours it looked like serious trouble could not be averted and that the streets of Huntington would be stained with the blood of many of her citizens. Marshal law was proclamed, all the reserve police as well as the fire department were placed on duty, and three companies of militia were called out. Finally a stream of water was turned into the crowd and it was dispersed.

Those arrested and who will be held on charges of inciting riot were Vaught Gilkerson, J. W. Mitchell, Frank Riley, Irvin Challenger, G. A. VanMeter, Albert Philips, R. Magee, J. Barber, Tom Blevins, Roscoe Johnson, 'Kid' Redmond, Arthur Underwood, J. T. Ryan, Clifford Wells, John Cole, Ralph Bailey, Pearl Newman, 'Bud' Kane. Unless they are able to give bond, they will be held in jail to await the action of the grand jury. Prosecutor Smith stated that he would vigorously prosecute all of those who had been arrested.
john-wayne-huntington-1910-08-29.A20:
PROBE RIOTING
HUNTINGTON MOB LEADERS MAY NOT BE THROUGH WITH FUN YET.
HUNTINGTON, W. Va., Aug. 31.—
The mob spirit that has prevailed in Huntington since Sunday night was dampened yesterday when a special grand jury was summoned to meet today to indict those arrested for participating in the riots.

Adjutant General Elliott arrived here yesterday afternoon from Charleston and assumed charge of the situation.

The three local companies of the State militia are on duty at the jail and no further outbreaks are anticipated.

All the saloons in the city were closed early yesterday evening and last night there was very little excitement.

The troops will remain on guard at the jail throughout the week.

The authorities will attempt to allay the public wrath by meting out speedy justice to the accused negroes. The grand jury which meets to-day, will indict Charles Clyburn for the murder of Harry Withrow, white railroad foreman, and the negro will be placed on trial Friday.

John Alliff, the husband of the woman whom John Wayne is accused of having criminally assaulted and then murdered was brought here from Hinton by Prosecuting Attorney Love, for the purpose of identifying Wayne. The accused negro was picked out by Alliff from a gang of a dozen negroes as the guilty man. Every effort was made to suppress the fact of identification, as it was feared that should this become known, another attack would be made on the jail.
john-wayne-huntington-1910-08-29.A21:
WILL IT EVER END-
As it is, Col- Roosevelt has "come back" with the Negro good and strong and, in proportion as the Colonel goes up Mr. Taft goes down.

The effort put forth by Governor Glasscock to save a Negro suspect from mob violence at Huntington, this week, was no less prompt efficient than the two instances previously commented upon in these columns, but we must confess that we are growing weary of this subject. Not mind you, that our chief executive can be too highly commended every time he exercises the powers of his office to preserve the good name of the State, but that the necessity for his doing so is becoming monotonously frequent.

We grow weary of these crimes and criminals who stir the public up to the point where it casts aside respect for the constituted authorities and attempts to take into its own hands the summary punishment of wrong doers. It no longer suffices to say that the law would be allowed to take up its course if the accused were white, that the black criminal should be accorded all the rights guaranteed by the constitution of the State and the Nation.

It is a condition and not a theory which confronts the Negro people in West Virginia. However much we may deplore the fact that the color of the skin of the accused is more often condemned than his crime, since that is the case, since the black criminal does not receive the tolerance of the white, the law-abiding element of the race looks forward to the day, though with but little hope, when criminality will be unknown among us.

The Advocate is anxious to see in the saddle a set of race leaders who can pull more than their own weight.

Dr. Booker T. Washington richly deserves the rest he is getting across
john-wayne-huntington-1910-08-29.A22:
MOB LEADERS
ARE INDICTED
MEN WHO LED IN RIOTOUS ACTS AT HUNTINGTON MUST STAND TRIAL.
HUNTINGTON, W. Va., Sept. 1. Since the State militia was called into action there have been no further riotous outbreaks in Huntington and the authorities do not anticipate any more trouble. The special grand jury which met yesterday afternoon to deal with the riot situation returned felony indictments last evening against Vaught Gilkeson, W. J. Mitchell and Chas. Turner, three alleged leaders of the mob that stormed the jail Monday night.

An indictment was also found against Charles Clyburn, the negro who is charged with murder of Harry Withrow and Clyburn will be placed on trial Friday morning. The grand jury will continue in session and take up the cases of others arrested for rioting but it is the general belief that these will be held only on misdemeanor charges.

John Wayne, the negro identified by John Alliff as the murderer of his wife near Hinton, will probably be taken to the penitentiary at Moundsville for safe keeping. He will be tried in Fayette county in October and since the news of his identification by Alliff became public, it is not regarded as safe to keep him here. The militia will be kept on duty until after the trial of Clyburn.
john-wayne-huntington-1910-08-29.A29:
TORNADO AT SMITH CENTER
Accompanied by Hail It Laid Waste Tracft One Mile Wide and Eight Long.

Smith Center, Kansas.—A tornado, combined with a terrific hail storm, laid waste an area a mile wide and eight or ten miles long north of this place.

Outbuildings were broken to chips, barns were wrecked and houses moved from their foundations. Three were entirely shorn of their foliage by the hail which, coming with the wind, mowed to earth all growing vegetation.

The loss will amount to many thousand dollars.

Martial Law For Negroes.

Huntington, W. Va.—Martial law was proclaimed here after three companies of the state militia had dispersed a crowd of over 1,500 rioters who were bent upon lynching John Wayne and Charles Clayburn, both negroes, now imprisoned in the county jail, charged with murder.
john-wayne-huntington-1910-08-29.A31: The failure of the jury to agree in the Clyburn case at Huntington will not help to quiet matters down much in that section. It is the law's delays that cause much of the mob spirit of which we have heard so much lately and a hung jury is one of the obstacles in the way of speedy justice.

poplarville-poplarville-1910-08.A1:
CHARGED WITH WHITE
CAPPING THE NEGROES
The cause of the trouble, it is thought was reached last night when Sheriff Rouse arrested two white men, William McLemore and Frank Parker, on a charge of white-capping, sworn to by V. D. Durham, a member of the above firm.

Mr. Durham says he has positive proof that these men marched one of his negro hands away from his place in the night time at the point of shot guns, and would not even give him time to get his clothing and see Mr. Durham.

It is hoped that these arrests will end this trouble as a scarcity of labor in the turpentine business at this time, when the harvest of the crop is in full blast, causes the loss of thousands of dollars in a very short time. The parties under arrest will be given a preliminary trial the last of this week.
